fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "NLP as reverse engineered charisma", "body": "Thomas Gorence frames neuro linguistic programming less as a doctrine than as a checklist you get by observing a charismatic person and indexing every successful behavior they have. He credits Richard Bandler and John Grinder as the originators, then notes that their split scattered the field into competing brands, trademarks and licensed trainer schemes that he compares to a pyramid. His own preference is to ignore the packaged models entirely and treat NLP as a Walmart combo bundle of borrowed techniques. Chance Garton pushes back gently, arguing that having a full model beats picking up social instincts piecemeal."}, {"title": "Anchoring, the technique underneath everything", "body": "The pair spend much of the hour on anchoring, which Thomas defines as putting someone into a charged state and then linking that state to a sensation. His examples run from a wedding song and a grandmother's perfume to burning sage before ritual, the tap method, and the McDonald's commercial that flashes its logo for one second after the happy family scene. He calls olfactory anchors the strongest because smell binds to memory hardest. Spatial anchoring gets a live demonstration, with Thomas charging one side of the frame with approval and the other with boredom while explaining he is doing it."}, {"title": "Mesmerism, hypnotism, and the MKUltra thread", "body": "Thomas traces NLP back through stage hypnotism to Franz Mesmer, animal magnetism and the idea of an energy field you could transfer between people, noting that hypnotism branched off rather than dissolving into modern psychology. He first encountered NLP through his own MKUltra research, then paid roughly six hundred dollars for a last minute seat at a Bandler seminar near his Florida apartment around 2005. Chance connects this to the occult read as cosmic psychology, where learning the mind dynamics of the individual means pulling the levers of the whole society, which is why fracturing one psyche scales."}, {"title": "Crowds, rhetoric, and manufactured consent", "body": "Citing Gustave Le Bon's The Crowd, Thomas argues a crowd is a single dumb person whose intelligence never exceeds the lowest common denominator, so a confident speaker with all the wrong information can still carry a room. After confidence comes the trivium, grammar, logic and rhetoric, which he points out is now taught almost exclusively in politics and sales. He extends this to media control, saying you no longer need a Bavarian Illuminati when six corporations, a think tank report written by former agency staff, and a short Zoom call will do. He adds that Mockingbird style retractions exploit the mind's blindness to negation."}, {"title": "Turning the toolbox on yourself", "body": "The most actionable stretch is Thomas explaining how to run these techniques on your own mind. He reframed brutal Disney commutes by casting the driver who cut him off as an uncle and the slow car ahead as grandma, then anchored that calm to how he held the wheel. He walks listeners through the swish method, zooming a joyful memory bigger and brighter while shrinking a cringe memory into blurry black and white, and builds a memory palace starting with a twenty foot childhood toy blocking the front door. Chance applies the same logic to breaking late night eating."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The Paranoid American Thomas Gorence returns to InnerVerse to articulate the arcane art of Neuro-Linguistic Programming, a set of techniques that can allegedly assist us in rewiring our minds to break unhealthy habits and adverse associations. What are the occult and magical origins of NLP, and how might these tactics be used for social engineering and mind control?
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the 2nd hour, on InnerVerse Plus, we dive deeper into NLP tactics, explore their relation to psychic/energy vampirism, discuss digital entrainment, and much more.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Mirroring as rapport and as a mirror of self", "body": "Thomas frames matching someone's speaking pace as meeting them where they process information, the way a good mediator walks into a shouting match, acknowledges the heat, and then tapers it down rather than demanding calm. He likens NLP to a cookbook you eventually outgrow until it becomes jazz. Chance opens up about his Leo ascendant, his Libra moon, and his Mayan sign of white magnetic mirror, admitting that as a young man he got depressed realizing he copied his friends' mannerisms, before Thomas offers a playful Simon Says test for spotting a salesman who is matching you."}, {"title": "What your eyes reveal when you remember", "body": "Thomas runs a live demonstration, asking Chance to picture the color of his parents' first car and then a glittering purple pumpkin, and points out that Chance glanced up and to the right without noticing. He explains that the direction differs from person to person but stays consistent for each, much like a poker tell, so recalling and constructing can be told apart. Chance wonders whether parents should learn their children's tells, Thomas finds that a little creepy, and both agree that accusing a spouse of lying over an eye movement is a recipe for conflict."}, {"title": "Love bombing and the psychic vampire", "body": "Thomas describes love bombing as a flood of affection that cannot be sustained, and points to the Barbie movie plan to deprogram the Kens by withdrawing adoration at its peak, echoing Fritz Springmeier's Monarch material. Chance holds up Joe Slate's Psychic Vampires with its Kirlian aura photos, then tells of a woman at a party who showered him with attention before cutting him down mid story. He argues the drop leaves an opening through which a vampire drains coherence, and that anyone who has fought to win the point, even in an imagined argument, has done a version of it."}, {"title": "Coolers, negging, and the swipe", "body": "Thomas brings up The Cooler with William H. Macy and the idea of a person whose bad luck drains a hot casino table, and Chance ties it to Joe Slate's photographs of dark tendrils puncturing a victim's aura. Thomas calls the pickup artist tactic of negging a form of psychic vampirism and compares it to salespeople who pull an offer away. At Chance's request he then takes up digital entrainment, describing how swiping with inertia and responses inside roughly 400 milliseconds build a feedback loop, a kinetic egregore that narrows focus into a trance."}, {"title": "Language as the borders of experience", "body": "Thomas walks through the meta model, answering a claim like nothing ever goes right by asking whether it really always does, and flags nominalizations such as justice, public health, and the war on terror. Chance adds modal operators, arguing that words like should and can't become the operating system for what you allow yourself to experience, and suggests setting the win at simply showing up. He admits a running joke with his wife about restaurants always being closed has made it happen more often. Thomas closes with a reframe of watching an argument from ever more distant theater seats."}]
